ta-l1d11q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 11, where Lombard treats the principle of the Holy Spirit's procession. He first shows that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son and then (Dist. 12) asks whether he proceeds equally from both. Lombard proves the truth and then addresses the Greek error that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. He states the Greek objection and his solution, and then brings the two sides into agreement of sense. The Greeks grant that the Spirit is 'of the Son', which is equivalent, and some Catholic Greek doctors expressly confess that he proceeds from the Son. Four articles are announced: whether the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son; whether from them as one or as several; if as one, whether as one in essence or in some notion; and whether Father and Son can be called one spirator.
claims: The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son; the Greek and Latin positions agree in sense though they differ in words.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3525.summary: First objection that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. Dionysius calls the Father the fontal deity and the Son and Spirit offshoots, flowers, and lights of the deity. An offshoot is not from an offshoot, nor a flower from a flower.
claims: Dionysius calls the Son and Spirit offshoots of the fontal Father.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3531.summary: Second objection, from the Passion of St Andrew, which confesses the Spirit 'proceeding from the Father and abiding in the Son'. What abides in one while proceeding from another does not proceed from the one in which it abides.
claims: The Spirit abides in the Son, so he does not proceed from him.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3537.summary: Third objection from Damascene: we say the Spirit is from the Father and call him the Father's Spirit; we do not say he is from the Son, though we call him the Son's Spirit.
claims: Damascene denies that the Spirit is from the Son.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3544.summary: Fourth objection, from a likeness. The bodily breath by which a vocal word is uttered does not proceed from the word; both proceed from the speaker. So the Spirit does not proceed from the Son, the Word, but both from the Father.
claims: Breath does not proceed from the spoken word.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3547.summary: Fifth objection. From the sun proceed splendour and heat, neither from the other. The Son is the Father's splendour (Heb. 1:3) and the Spirit is like heat, being love.
claims: Splendour and heat proceed independently from the sun.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3550.summary: Sixth objection. What proceeds bodily proceeds from one place into another, not from both. So the Spirit proceeds from the Father into the Son, not from Father and Son.
claims: Bodily procession is from one place into another.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3553.summary: Seventh objection. Nothing simple can be from two, otherwise the effect would be simpler than the cause. The Spirit is simple.
claims: A simple effect cannot come from two causes.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3556.summary: Eighth objection. The Spirit agrees with the Father no less than the Son and is of no less dignity. If the Son shares with the Father in spirating the Spirit, the Spirit would share with the Father in begetting the Son, which is false.
claims: Equality of dignity would require symmetry in production.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3559.summary: Ninth objection. Either the Father spirates the Spirit perfectly or not. If not, the Father is imperfect; if so, another spirator is superfluous, and nothing in God is superfluous.
claims: A perfect spirator makes a second spirator superfluous.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3563.summary: Notes that many authorities in Lombard's text support the contrary.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3566.summary: Sed contra from the likeness of the image. In the soul, which bears the image of the Trinity, love, which represents the Spirit, proceeds from knowledge, which represents the Son. So in God the Spirit proceeds from the Son.
claims: In the image, love proceeds from knowledge.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3569.summary: Second sed contra. All love proceeds from the lover, and the Spirit is the love of Father and Son (Damascene), so he proceeds from both as their love.
claims: Love proceeds from the lover, and the Spirit is the love of both.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3572.summary: Thomas's determination: the Spirit simply proceeds from the Son. If this is removed, the distinction of Son and Spirit is inevitably removed. Since the persons are distinguished by nothing absolute, all their distinction must be by relations of origin, and if Son and Spirit were not distinguished by one being from the other, they would be one person. Nor could they be distinguished merely by different modes of proceeding from the Father, nature for the Son and will for the Spirit. That difference would either be a relational opposition, which returns to the same point, or a difference in something absolute. A real absolute difference would mean composition in God, and a merely conceptual one cannot distinguish persons (Dist. 2). Since the Son is not from the Spirit, the Spirit is from the Son.
claims: The Spirit proceeds from the Son, since otherwise Son and Spirit could not be distinguished.
Divine persons are distinguished only by opposed relations of origin.
Different modes of procession from the Father alone cannot distinguish Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3575.summary: Reply to the first objection. These are symbolic expressions, and symbolic theology is not argumentative, as Dionysius himself says in the letter to Titus. The likeness holds in some respect, that the flowers are from one, but not in all.
claims: Symbolic theology does not yield arguments.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3578.summary: Reply to the second objection. The Spirit is said to abide in the Son not because he is distinct from him there. The spirative power is in the Father and, from the Father, in the Son, like everything the Son has, and it abides there and goes no further, since the Spirit has the power not to spirate but to be spirated. Alternatively, it refers to the Son in his assumed nature, in which nothing opposed the Spirit's grace, so the Spirit rests in him as he dwells in the saints.
claims: The spirative power abides in the Son and goes no further, since the Spirit does not spirate.
Alternatively, the Spirit rests in Christ's human nature.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3582.summary: Reply to the third objection. Damascene is not followed here, since he lived when the Greek–Latin controversy began. He does not deny that the Spirit is from the Son, but declines to affirm it because it was still in doubt among the Greeks.
claims: Damascene did not deny the filioque but left it in doubt.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3585.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. There are two words, vocal and mental, with two corresponding spirits: bodily breath to the vocal word and the spirit of inner love to the mental word. In his eternal generation the Word is like the mental word, so the Spirit proceeds from the Word as love from the mental word. As incarnate, the Son is like the vocal word, and as a voice is formed by breathed air, the Word's incarnation was accomplished by the Spirit's operation.
claims: As eternal Word, the Son is like a mental word, from which love proceeds.
As incarnate, the Son is like a vocal word, formed through the Spirit.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3588.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. The likeness assumes something false: according to the philosophers heat proceeds from splendour, and Avicenna says the sun heats lower things only through its light.
claims: Heat proceeds from light, so the analogy supports the filioque.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3591.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. 'Procession' is said properly in God, as 'generation' is, so it is not taken from the likeness of local procession, which would make it metaphorical. It means going out from a principle. Not everything from a principle proceeds into another; something proceeds as self-subsistent, and so the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son.
claims: Divine procession means going out from a principle, not local motion.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3594.summary: Reply to the seventh objection. Something simple cannot proceed from several things diverse in essence with diverse operations. But Father and Son spirate the Spirit by the power of one nature in one spiration, so the one spirated is simple.
claims: Father and Son spirate by one power and one spiration, so the Spirit remains simple.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3597.summary: Reply to the eighth objection. The Spirit cannot share with the Father in begetting the Son, for two reasons. First, the Son proceeds by way of nature, through generation, and an act of nature belongs to one alone, whereas the Spirit proceeds as love by way of will, and several can be united in will toward one act. Second, it would contradict the Spirit's property of proceeding from Father and Son as love, since two cannot be principles of each other. As the Father does not communicate paternity to the Son so that the Son begets himself, so he does not communicate it to the Spirit so that the Spirit begets the Son. It is as unfitting, or more so, for something to be begotten by what it is the principle of as to be begotten by itself.
claims: An act of nature belongs to one principle; several can unite in an act of will.
Two persons cannot be principles of each other.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3601.summary: Reply to the last objection. The Father spirates the Spirit perfectly. But every perfection of the Father not conflicting with his property is communicated to the Son, since only relation of origin distinguishes them. So as he communicates the perfection of deity, he communicates the perfection of spirating. The Son spirates not because of the Father's imperfection but because of the Son's perfection, having the Father's whole perfection. By the same argument one could claim the Son is not God or does not create.
claims: The Son spirates because he receives all the Father's perfection compatible with his property, not because the Father is imperfect.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3613.summary: First argument that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son not as one. He proceeds as their bond or union, and a bond is of distinct things.
claims: A bond joins distinct things.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3616.summary: Second argument. Father and Son love each other both as one in essence and as distinct persons. As one in essence they love by essential love, so as distinct persons they love by a love proceeding from them, the Spirit. So the Spirit proceeds from them as distinct persons.
claims: Father and Son love each other as distinct persons by a proceeding love.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3619.summary: Third argument. Acts belong to supposits, so spirating, as an act of Father and Son, belongs to them as distinct supposits.
claims: Acts belong to supposits.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3623.summary: Contrary argument. Father and Son are distinguished by paternity and filiation. If the Spirit proceeded from them as distinct, he would proceed from the Father by paternity and from the Son by filiation. Then the Father would be related by paternity both to Son and Spirit, and both processions would be the same, which is impossible.
claims: Procession from distinct persons as distinct would make paternity relate the Father to both Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3626.summary: Second contrary argument. Nothing simple proceeds from several unless they are one in essence and operation (Dist. 8, q. 5, a. 2), and the Spirit is simple, so he proceeds from Father and Son as one.
claims: A simple effect proceeds from several only as one in essence and operation.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3629.summary: Thomas's determination. Every act is referred originally to two things: the agent, the supposit (a man or a fire), and the principle of action, some substantial or accidental form in it. 'Inasmuch as' can express the condition of the agent or of the principle of action. As to the agent, the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as several and distinct persons, since he proceeds from them, several and distinct. As to the principle of action, he proceeds from them as one, since an operation comes only from one principle, so there must be something one in Father and Son that is the principle of the one, simple act of spirating, by which the one, simple Spirit proceeds.
claims: The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as several agents but from one principle of action.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3632.summary: This resolves all the arguments; what the one common principle in Father and Son is will be shown in the next article.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3644.summary: First argument that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as one in nature. Nature is communicated only by an act of nature, and the Spirit receives the whole divine nature by proceeding, as the Son does by being born. So the principle of the act by which nature is communicated to him is the nature. Anselm says it is ridiculous to hold that the whole essence of Father and Son is in the Spirit because of relation rather than because of essence.
claims: Nature is communicated only by an act of nature.
Anselm: the essence is in the Spirit because of essence, not relation.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3647.summary: Second argument. The Spirit proceeds as love, which implies a procession of will, so from Father and Son as one in will, and will, being absolute, belongs to the nature.
claims: Will, as absolute, belongs to the nature.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3650.summary: Third argument. A property takes its number from its supposit, so two supposits cannot have numerically one property or notion. Father and Son are distinct supposits, so they cannot agree in one notion, and the Spirit proceeds from them as one in essence.
claims: Two supposits cannot share numerically one property.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3654.summary: Sed contra. The Spirit shares in the power of the divine essence as the Son does. If Father and Son spirate as one in nature, the Spirit would spirate himself along with them, which is impossible.
claims: If spiration were by the essence as such, the Spirit would spirate himself.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3657.summary: Anticipates the reply that the Spirit's property conflicts with this. Properties do not distinguish or determine the essence, only the person, so whatever belongs to the essence in Father and Son belongs to it in the Spirit.
claims: Properties do not determine the essence.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3660.summary: Thomas's determination. Father and Son spirate the Spirit as one in spirative power. Spirative power, like generative power (Dist. 7), is a mean between essence and property, since it signifies the essence under the aspect of a property: a notional act proceeds from the essence not as from an agent but as from that by which the agent acts. Generation proceeds from the essence not as essence but as paternity; if essence and paternity differed, generation would proceed from paternity immediately and from essence as first principle. Similarly, spiration proceeds from the essence not as spirator but as principle of spiration, insofar as the essence has the character of a notion common to Father and Son, called common spiration. So the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as one in essence and in a notion, common spiration.
claims: Father and Son spirate as one in spirative power, the essence under the aspect of common spiration.
Notional acts proceed from the essence as that by which, under the aspect of a property.
concepts: essence under the aspect of property

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3663.summary: Reply to the first argument. Generally, nature is communicated by an act of nature, but a determinate communication must be by an act of nature taken under a proper aspect. So communication by spiration is an act of the divine nature as it has the character of spiration. Anselm means that the nature must in some way be the principle of a procession terminating in the nature, since there is a quasi-univocal communication: God proceeds from God as fire from fire.
claims: Spiration communicates the nature as an act of nature under the aspect of spiration.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3666.summary: Reply to the second argument, following from the first: the same holds of will as of essence.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3669.summary: Reply to the third argument. Supposits distinct in essence cannot share one notion. But if their essence is one, their operation is one, and since a relation arises conceptually from an operation, their relation is also one. So Father and Son can agree in one relative property.
claims: Father and Son, sharing one essence and operation, can share one relative property, common spiration.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3673.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Spirating comes from the essence not as essence but as it has the character of common spiration. The essence does not have that character in the Spirit, so it does not follow that the Spirit spirates by his essence.
claims: The essence in the Spirit lacks the character of common spiration.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3676.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. If a property in a person were other than the essence, it would necessarily determine it, per se or per accidens. But because it is really the same as the essence, it does not come to it as restricting or determining it. Still, under one property the essence is the principle of an act of which it is not the principle under another, as it is the principle of willing under the aspect of will and of knowing under the aspect of knowledge, without being really determined or distinguished. So under the aspect of common spiration the essence in Father and Son is the principle of spirating, and it is not so in the Spirit, where the essence is not common spiration.
claims: Properties, being really identical with the essence, do not determine it, yet the essence is a principle of different acts under different properties.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3689.summary: First argument that Father and Son are one spirator. 'Spirator' implies only unity in the act of spirating, and Father and Son spirate by one act, so they are one spirator, as they are one God by the unity of deity.
claims: Unity of act would make them one spirator.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3692.summary: Second argument. Father and Son agree in the act of creating as in spirating, and for that reason are called one creator, so they should be called one spirator.
claims: Father and Son are one creator.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3695.summary: Third argument. 'Principle' names a relation following the act by which something is a principle, and Father and Son are called one principle of the Spirit (Dist. 29), so they should also be called one spirator.
claims: Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3699.summary: Sed contra. Whoever spirates is spirating; Father and Son spirate, so they are spirating and spirators of the Spirit.
claims: Those who spirate are spirators.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3702.summary: Thomas's determination. An act takes its number from its supposits, so a verb signifying substance by way of act is said of several persons in the plural, though the essence is one ('I and the Father are one', John 10:30). Act is signified in the verb, the participle, and the verbal noun, but the participle comes closer to substance than the verb, and the verbal noun closer still. So we do not say that Father and Son 'spirates', or are 'spirating' or 'a spirator' in the singular, but that they spirate and are spirating and spirators. Though the act is one, the more a term signifies act, the less properly it can be predicated in the singular.
claims: Acts take number from supposits, so Father and Son 'spirate' and are 'spirators' in the plural.
The more a term signifies act, the less properly it is predicated in the singular.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3708.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though the act is one, when it is signified as going out from several supposits it must be signified in the plural, since act takes number from supposits.
claims: An act going out from several supposits is signified plurally.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3711.summary: Reply to the second argument. Creation is an act of the three persons not as distinct but as united in essence; even with the distinction of persons removed in thought, creation would remain. So the three are one creator, though not 'one creating', since the verbal noun is further from act than the participle. Spiration belongs to several supposits in a way as they are distinct, so even in the verbal noun the act must be signified in the plural.
claims: Creation belongs to the persons as one in essence, so they are one creator.
Spiration belongs to the persons as in some way distinct, so they are spirators, not one spirator.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3714.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Principle' names not an act but only a relation, and because Father and Son are related by one relation to the Spirit, they are called one principle of the Spirit, but not one spirator.
claims: 'Principle' names a relation, so Father and Son are one principle but not one spirator.

ta-l1d11q1-d1e3723.summary: An expositio textus. (1) Lombard's proof from 'God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts' seems insufficient, since the Greeks grant that the Spirit is 'of the Son' but not 'from the Son'. But a genitive must express some relationship, and the only one that can hold here is origin, since only such relations distinguish persons, so the Spirit must originate from the Son. (2) The proof from 'whom I will send you from the Father' seems to concern only the temporal procession, which the Greeks grant is from the Son. But the temporal procession includes the eternal (Dist. 15), so the one from whom he proceeds temporally is the one from whom he proceeds eternally. (3) The anathema on teaching 'otherwise' means teaching something contrary. What is not contrary to Scripture is its truth (Anselm), and not everything to be believed is explicit in the Creed, which does not mention the descent into hell; the Spirit's procession is implicit there in the distinction of persons. (4) To the Greek question how the Latins dared add the filioque: it was necessary, as the Greek error showed, and the Roman Church has the authority to convene a synod to express what was implicit in the articles of faith.
claims: The genitive 'Spirit of the Son' can only signify a relation of origin.
The temporal procession includes the eternal, so the Spirit sent by the Son proceeds eternally from him.
The filioque makes explicit what is implicit in the Creed, and the Roman Church had authority to add it.

ta-l1d11q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 11 maps Lombard's proof that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son and his treatment of the Greek objection, which agrees with the Latin position in sense. It announces four articles on the filioque and on the unity of the spirating principle.

ta-l1d11q1-Dd1e3517.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Spirit proceeds from the Son. Against Dionysian, hagiographical, Damascene, analogical, and rational objections, Thomas holds that the Spirit simply proceeds from the Son. Persons are distinguished only by opposed relations of origin, so without the filioque Son and Spirit could not be distinguished, and different modes of procession from the Father would not suffice. The replies dismiss symbolic arguments and explain that the spirative power 'abides' in the Son. They note Damascene's era of doubt and reread the analogies of word, breath, and sun in favour of the filioque. Father and Son spirate by one power, so the Spirit remains simple. The Spirit cannot share in begetting, since nature acts from one principle and two cannot be principles of each other, and the Son spirates from his own perfection, not from the Father's lack.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as the Father.
Without the filioque, Son and Spirit could not be distinguished.

ta-l1d11q1-Dd1e3605.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as one or as several. Thomas distinguishes the agent (supposit) from the principle of action (form). As agents, Father and Son spirate as several, distinct persons. As principle, they spirate as one, since one simple act requires one principle.
claims: The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son as two agents but one principle.

ta-l1d11q1-Dd1e3636.summary: Article 3 asks whether Father and Son are one in essence or in a notion as principle of spiration. Thomas holds that they spirate as one in spirative power, which is the essence under the aspect of common spiration, a notion common to Father and Son. Notional acts proceed from the essence as that by which, under the aspect of a property. The Spirit does not spirate himself, because the essence in him is not common spiration. Two persons can share one relative property because they share one essence and operation, and properties do not determine the essence.
claims: Father and Son spirate as one in essence under the aspect of common spiration.
The Spirit does not spirate, because the essence in him is not common spiration.

ta-l1d11q1-Dd1e3681.summary: Article 4 asks whether Father and Son are one spirator. Because acts take number from supposits, and the more a term signifies act the less it can be singular, Father and Son 'spirate' and are 'spirators' in the plural, though by one act. They are one creator, since creation belongs to them as one in essence. They are one principle of the Spirit, since 'principle' names a relation, not an act, but they are not one spirator.
claims: Father and Son are spirators, not one spirator, but they are one principle of the Spirit.

ta-l1d11q1-Dd1e3718.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 11 defends Lombard's scriptural proofs of the filioque. The genitive 'Spirit of the Son' can only signify origin, and the temporal procession includes the eternal. It justifies the Latin addition to the Creed as making explicit what was implicit, by the Roman Church's synodal authority.
claims: The genitive 'of the Son' signifies origin; the filioque addition makes explicit what was implicit in the Creed.

ta-l1d11q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 11 defends the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. Article 1 argues that without the filioque Son and Spirit could not be distinguished, since divine persons differ only by opposed relations of origin. Patristic and analogical objections are answered, and Damascene's reticence is explained historically. Articles 2–3 hold that Father and Son spirate as two agents but one principle, as one in spirative power, which is the essence under the aspect of common spiration. Article 4 holds that because acts take number from supposits, Father and Son are 'spirators' and not 'one spirator', though they are one creator and one principle of the Spirit. The Expositio defends the scriptural proofs and the Latin addition of the filioque as an explicitation of the faith authorized by the Roman Church.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, which is required for the distinction of Son and Spirit.
Father and Son spirate as one principle, in common spiration, but are plural spirators.
The filioque makes explicit what is implicit in the Creed.
